title: Hydrogen embrittlement risk of automotive steel
abstract: Abstract Advanced high-strength steels have wide applications in automotive body-in-white components due to their combination of high strength, fracture resistance, and low cost. However, its further promotion is restricted by the critical challenge from hydrogen embrittlement, especially in the ultra-high strength steels. To study the origin of hydrogen embrittlement and provide inspiration for future research, this review systematically summarizes hydrogen embrittlement mechanisms and advanced hydrogen characterization techniques. Evaluation methods are discussed for assessing hydrogen embrittlement risk. The hydrogen embrittlement behaviors of quenched & partitioned steels, medium-Mn steels, press-hardened steels, and tailor-welded blanks are analyzed, highlighting the roles of microstructure, hydrogen traps, and processing routes. This work provides insights for future research aimed at enhancing the hydrogen resistance of advanced high-strength steels for the automotive industry.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Since the beginning of the twenty-first century, China's automotive industry has entered a period of rapid development. After 2008, China became and has continuously remained the world's largest producer and consumer of automobiles [ 1 ]. In 2024, China's automobile market accounted for one-third of the global market share, with the automotive economy becoming a vital pillar of the national economy [ 1 ,  2 – 3 ]. To simultaneously ensure the prosperity of the automotive industry and restrict greenhouse gas emissions, lightweight technology is always the central topic of the automotive industry and the focus of study. This is because the reduction of vehicle mass effectively improves the fuel economy of automobiles [ 4 ,  5 ], which limits the greenhouse gas emission of fuel vehicles or extends the travelling range of electric vehicles. Therefore, steel is an excellent material for body in white (BIW) of vehicles since the early twentieth century due to its combination of strength, ductility, and fracture toughness [ 6 ]. In recent years, the development of advanced high-strength steel (AHSS) has further amplified the advantages of steels in BIW manufacturing [ 7 ,  8 ], as its ultra-high strength results in 30–50% lightweighting effects when compared to traditional low strength cold rolled carbon steel [ 9 ,  10 ,  11 – 12 ]. The revolution of jointing technology, like tailor-welded blank (TWB), realizes an optimized balance among strength, ductility, corrosion resistance, and lightweighting at multiple safety components of BIW, including A-pillar, B-pillar, bumper and roof rail [ 13 ].

However, during the manufacturing and service of steels, hydrogen is induced into the materials [ 14 ]. As the smallest atom, hydrogen easily diffuses from the surface into the interior of steel and distributes inhomogeneously within the material due to the heterogeneity of the microstructure and the localized concentration of stress. The interactions among hydrogen, susceptible microstructure defects, and complex stress conditions mutually contribute to hydrogen embrittlement of steels, manifested as degradation of fracture toughness and premature brittle fracture at stress levels below the ultimate tensile strength or even the yield stress. This hydrogen embrittlement risk becomes even more severe with the increase in the strength of steel. It is reported that 2 GPa press-hardened steel (PHS) exhibits a significantly greater risk of hydrogen embrittlement compared to 1.5 GPa PHS, which negates the weight-saving benefits of 2 GPa PHS when the hydrogen content exceeds 0.5 wppm [ 15 ]. Considering the urgent needs of the automotive industry for ultra-high-strength structural materials, the hydrogen embrittlement risk has become one of the most critical challenges for the safe application of AHSS in BIW.

To better study and understand hydrogen embrittlement of materials, reliable hydrogen tracking and measurement methods are necessary. However, microstructure-specific hydrogen tracking is always a challenge for researchers. This is due to the low concentration (typically 0.1 to several wppm), high diffusivity (> 1 × 10 –5  mm 2 /s) of hydrogen in martensitic steel at room temperature [ 16 ,  17 – 18 ]. To overcome these obstacles and realize microstructure-scale hydrogen tracking, multiple hydrogen tracking methods have been developed to facilitate both qualitative and quantitative characterization of hydrogen in bulk and microstructures of materials, including secondary ion mass spectroscopy (SIMS), hydrogen microprint technique (HMT), scanning Kelvin probe force microscopy (SKPFM), and atom probe tomography (APT). Besides, although thermal desorption spectrometry (TDS) cannot provide spatial resolution of hydrogen in the material, it is still a powerful tool to provide microstructure-sensitive information on hydrogen content.

Except for characterization methods of hydrogen distribution, the evaluation methods for hydrogen embrittlement risk are also critical for the study of hydrogen embrittlement. Currently, the slow-strain-rate tensile test (SSRT) is the most widely applied hydrogen embrittlement risk evaluation method for both academic and industrial communities [ 19 ]. SSRT is renowned for its minimal time consumption, high repeatability of results, and advantages in facilitating mechanism studies. However, SSRT only evaluates the hydrogen embrittlement risk of steel under a uniaxial tensile stress state, while in real-life applications, the steel is experiencing complex stress states. Therefore, slow-strain-rate bending and slow-strain-rate biaxial tensile tests have been utilized to evaluate the hydrogen embrittlement risk of steels in recent studies [ 17 ]. Besides, constant load tests (CLT) and four-point bending tests (FPB) are also widely utilized for the evaluation of the hydrogen embrittlement risk of steels [ 20 ].

To mitigate the high hydrogen embrittlement risk of high-strength steels and promote their applications in the automotive industry, multiple strategies have been proposed to enhance the hydrogen embrittlement resistance of high-strength steels. For example, through phase distribution and morphology designing, the hydrogen embrittlement fracture of quench and partitioning (Q&P) steel (typical strength level 700–1200 MPa and carbon content 0.1–0.3 wt.%) is alleviated [ 21 ]. By low temperature tempering, the internal stress of ultra-high strength PHS (typical strength level 1500–2200 MPa and carbon content 0.2–0.35 wt.%) is largely relaxed, thereby significantly improving the hydrogen embrittlement resistance of that PHS [ 22 ]. Most importantly, the strategy of introducing hydrogen traps to limit the aggregation of diffusible hydrogen has been demonstrated to be highly effective and widely adopted in mitigating the risk of hydrogen embrittlement in materials [ 23 ]. Recently, the introduction of Nb, V, and Mo carbides effectively improved the hydrogen embrittlement resistance of PHS [ 24 ], providing a wide range of pathways for researchers and engineers to mitigate the hydrogen embrittlement risk of high-strength steel. Besides, the chemical heterogeneity strategy significantly improves the hydrogen embrittlement risk of medium-manganese steel (MMS) and broadens the horizon for microstructure engineering.

Although a wide variety of steels are used in the automotive industry, this review intentionally focuses on Q&P steel, MMS, PHS, and TWB, due to their fast development and high application potential in automotive industry. To facilitate the synthesis of current mature strategies for enhancing hydrogen embrittlement resistance in automotive steels and to provide references and inspiration for future research, this review will systematically summarize the hydrogen embrittlement mechanisms, existing hydrogen characterization techniques, hydrogen embrittlement assessment methods, and related research findings on multiple categories of high-strength steels.

sections.heading: Hydrogen embrittlement mechanisms, characterization, and evaluation
Hydrogen embrittlement mechanisms
paragraphs: Since the first identification of the hydrogen embrittlement phenomenon of iron in 1875 [ 25 ], intensive research has been conducted to study the fracture mechanism of this reversible phenomenon [ 14 ,  26 ,  27 ,  28 – 29 ]. Multiple hydrogen embrittlement mechanisms have been proposed, although an accurate and comprehensive prediction of hydrogen-induced fracture of steel based on mechanisms remains a significant challenge.

Although brittle hydride formation at a hydrostatic stress concentration zone is an important mechanism for hydrogen embrittlement in metallic materials, the condition for hydride formation in steel is extremely harsh [ 30 ], making this mechanism rarely observed in steels. The existence of hydrogen atoms can weaken the interatomic bonds of Fe due to the donation of the 1s electron of hydrogen to the unfilled 3d shell of iron atoms [ 31 ]. This mechanism is named hydrogen-enhanced decohesion (HEDE). The weakened interatomic bonds facilitate dislocation movement and hydrogen migration via dislocation-mediated transport to grain boundaries and other defects, thereby promoting the decohesion of grain boundaries and the intergranular failure of steels [ 32 ].

Hydrogen solute in the iron matrix assists the movement of dislocations and causes a reduction of shear stress [ 33 ]. The enhanced movement of dislocations promotes the localization of deformation around the critical crack tips. Compared to the hydrogen-free state, the microvoid-coalescence (MVC) [ 34 ] is much more localized, and the size of the dimple is much smaller. The moving dislocations act as hydrogen carriers that assist the local concentration of hydrogen around the crack tip, which in turn promotes the localization of strain. The highly localized strain leads to the initiation and propagation of critical microcracks. This mechanism is named hydrogen-enhanced localized plasticity (HELP) [ 35 ]. This mechanism accounts for both transgranular and intergranular fracture, depending on the hydrogen segregation conditions.

The adsorption of hydrogen on the crack tip facilitates the nucleation of a dislocation there due to its weakening effect on interatomic bonds. The shearing of atoms and the formation of surface steps become easier due to the weakened interatomic bonds. The nucleated dislocations then move into the material under the applied stress. This emission of dislocations from the crack tip into the material leads to the degradation of the fracture toughness of the material and promotes brittle fracture. This mechanism is named adsorption-induced dislocation emission (AIDE) [ 36 ]. When material is in a hydrogen-free state, the crack propagation process is dominated by the egress of dislocations, which limits the number of dislocations that produce crack advance. Due to the lack of dislocations assisting crack advance, the growth of the crack depends on the large strain ahead of the crack tip. Therefore, a high density of deep dimples is formed on the fractography. On the contrary, when the material is in a hydrogen-rich environment, dislocation emission becomes much more pronounced. Many more dislocations participate in the propagation of the crack rather than forming large strain ahead of the crack tip due to the injection of dislocations on suitable slip planes, for example, {110} planes for body-centered cubic (BCC) structure [ 17 ]. Consequently, the density and size of dimples are much smaller than materials in the hydrogen-free state. The schematics illustrating the crack propagation process in the hydrogen-free state and hydrogen-rich state (AIDE-induced cracking) have been shown in Fig.  1 . Both intergranular and transgranular fractures could be induced by AIDE. Interestingly, for transgranular fracture, the alternating-slip phenomenon has been identified [ 17 ,  37 ]. This is because the alternating injection of dislocations on two different planes could minimize the back-stress from the former emitted dislocations. Fig. 1 a  Schematic of dislocation egress-induced crack propagation mechanism.  b  The AIDE resulted brittle fracture mechanism. Reprinted from [ 33 ] with permission. Copyright 2012 De Gruyter Brill

HELP, HEDE, and AIDE are important hydrogen embrittlement mechanisms in steels. A schematic to exhibit the three mechanisms is shown in Fig.  2 . Fig. 2 Schematic of three critical hydrogen embrittlement mechanisms of steel. Reprinted from [ 38 ]. CC BY-NC-ND 4.0

Except for the above-mentioned three hydrogen embrittlement mechanisms, the hydrogen pressure theory also explains the brittle fracture of steels. Under the influence of the driving force from the stress gradient or the hydrogen activation energy difference, hydrogen tends to gather around defects of the material. The recombination of hydrogen atoms produces hydrogen molecules, which significantly increases the volume of solute hydrogen. The pressure from hydrogen molecules applies extra stress to these vulnerable defects and promotes their cracking or expansion. This theory successfully explains the observed hydrogen blistering phenomenon in steels. Furthermore, hydrogen not only assists the movement of dislocations but also facilitates the formation of vacancies [ 39 ]. The plastic strain of steel substantially increases the dislocation density of the material, and hydrogen effectively enhances this process. A large number of these newly formed defects have been proven to be vacancies. These vacancies gather ahead of the critical crack tip and lead to the localization of strain concentration ahead of the crack tip, thereby resulting in the degradation of the fracture toughness of the material. This newly proposed hydrogen embrittlement fracture mechanism is named the hydrogen-enhanced strain-induced vacancies (HESIV) mechanism.

sections.heading: Hydrogen characterization methods
paragraphs: To systematically study the hydrogen’s role in the brittle fracture of steels, the microstructure scale hydrogen detection and mapping are essential. With the development of characterization techniques, these kinds of measurement and mapping have become feasible. TDS is widely used in measuring the total hydrogen content in material, the specific hydrogen content in different hydrogen trapping sites with different hydrogen trapping energies. The hydrogen desorption peaks in different hydrogen trapping sites in pure iron are shown in Fig.  3 . It shows that the desorption peak of solid solute hydrogen is at cryogenic temperature, which indicates the extremely low hydrogen trapping energy of the matrix of pure iron. On the contrary, the defects of iron, such as grain boundaries and vacancies, have much larger hydrogen trapping energy and corresponding higher hydrogen desorption peaks. To better measure the weakly trapped hydrogen in different trapping sites, cryogenic TDS has been developed [ 40 ,  41 ]. Fig. 3 The hydrogen desorption profile of different hydrogen trapping sites in pure iron. Reprinted from [ 16 ] with permission. Copyright 2017 Sage

SIMS provides a 3D mapping of hydrogen distribution in the specimen at a resolution of the micron scale [ 43 ]. The high-energy ion beam is used to serially section the sample surface, and the emitted ions are collected and measured by a mass filter and counter. Based on the collected ions, the distribution of deuterium is decided. Due to the serial section of the ion beam, SIMS provides in-depth spatial resolution of hydrogen. To measure the hydrogen distribution inside the material with high hydrogen diffusivity, for example, the ferritic steel, cryogenic SIMS measurement has been utilized recently to limit the movement of hydrogen and provide better resolution [ 43 ].

To realize higher nanometer-scale resolution characterization of hydrogen, SKPFM has been utilized. The detection of hydrogen in this method is based on the theory that the surface potential of the material decreases with the increase of local hydrogen content [ 16 ]. The probe of atomic force microscopy (AFM) measures the surface potential of the target sample, and the local decrease of surface potential is correlated to the local concentration of hydrogen. It has been reported that the coating of the sample surface by a thin palladium film significantly improves the quality of hydrogen measurement: the released hydrogen is stored in palladium, which has a much lower chemical potential. This significantly extends the observation time window; the formation of oxide films on the sample surface is always a major distraction for SKPFM, and the application of palladium coating effectively resolves this issue. Figure  5  shows the measurement of SKPFM on the surface of a duplex stainless steel (Fe-23.16Cr-2.64Ni-1.29Mn-0.41Si-0.23Mo (in wt.%)). The duplex stainless steel sample has been charged under −1200 mV/SCE for 24 h in the sodium chloride aqueous solution (30 g/L). In Fig.  5 b, the potential mapping indicates that the hydrogen content diffusing from the ferrite and austenite to the exterior is very minimal and nearly undetectable. After 11 h, the hydrogen diffusing from the ferrite to the exterior of the material significantly increases; however, the hydrogen diffusing from the austenite remains very low (Fig.  5 c). This contrast is due to the significantly different hydrogen diffusivity between these two phases. After an even longer time (Fig.  5 d), this contrast becomes even larger. Therefore, SKPFM not only provides spatial resolution of hydrogen, but also enables the time resolution of hydrogen distribution in the sample surface. Fig. 5 a  Phase identification of austenite and ferrite in the duplex steel. Potential mapping of the surface in  a  by SKPFM at  b  0.5 h,  c  11 h, and  d  59 h after the electrochemical hydrogen charging. Reprinted from [ 44 ] with permission. Copyright 2019 Elsevier

Currently, the APT technique provides the best spatial resolution of hydrogen distribution in steels. In the best condition, it can realize the lattice parameter scale resolution. It needs to be pointed out that the hydrogen loss due to hydrogen diffusion at room temperature strongly influences the reliability of the characterization result; therefore cryogenic condition is necessary for the reliable characterization of hydrogen. The detection of deuterium in a ferritic steel (Fe-0.096C-1.6Mn-0.026Si-0.51Mo-0.25V-0.05Al-0.056Nb (in wt.%)) has been shown in Fig.  6 . It is clear that the charged deuterium concentrates around the vanadium carbides. These results support the theory that the introduction of atomic-scale hydrogen traps effectively limits the diffusion of hydrogen, therefore enhancing the material’s hydrogen embrittlement resistance [ 45 ]. Fig. 6 APT measured deuterium distribution in ferritic steel. Reprinted from [ 30 ] with permission. Copyright 2025 Elsevier

The HMT method visualizes the distribution of hydrogen on a sample surface by leveraging the hydrogen-assisted reduction of silver ions from a solution onto it. HMT is a very helpful supplement for SKPFM and APT due to its convenient experimental process. Its characterization scale ranges from microstructure-interface segregation to millimeter-scale hydrogen partition. The example of hydrogen distribution mapping on a sample surface is shown in Fig.  7 . In that study, a 2-GPa grade AlSi-coated PHS was bent to 8.5°  and then unloaded. Subsequently, the sample was soaked in KAg(CN) 2  solution for silver reduction. The SEM image of the surface of that sample is shown in Fig.  7 b. For comparison, an undeformed sample was also soaked in KAg(CN) 2  solution, and its surface is shown in Fig.  7 a. The HMT clearly demonstrates hydrogen segregation at the crack tip after the bending of the material. Fig. 7 a  SEM image of materials in their initial state after HMT.  b  SEM image of material bent to 8.5° after HMT. The white particles are silver particles. Reprinted from [ 17 ] with permission. Copyright 2025 Elsevier

sections.heading: Hydrogen embrittlement risk evaluation methods
paragraphs: Although hydrogen embrittlement risk is of great importance for the development of high-strength steels, there is currently no mature and quantifiable method available in both academia and industry to assess it. Multiple evaluation methods, with their unique advantages and disadvantages, are simultaneously utilized for proper evaluation of materials’ hydrogen embrittlement risk. Currently, there is no universally optimal assessment method; instead, the most appropriate approach can only be selected by considering the actual operating conditions of the material. This allows for a more realistic evaluation of the hydrogen embrittlement risk experienced during practical usage.

Pre-charge slow strain rate tensile (SSRT) test is the most utilized method for hydrogen embrittlement risk evaluation [ 46 ]. Multiple options are available for the hydrogen charge. The most commonly used method for hydrogen charging is the electrochemical hydrogen charging method. 3 wt.% NaCl + 0.3 wt.% NH 4 SCN aqueous solution [ 47 ] or 0.1 mol/L NaOH aqueous solution [ 48 ,  49 ]. The purpose of adding NH 4 SCN into aqueous solution is to increase the hydrogen entry efficiency by tailoring the activation energy of hydrogen adsorption and absorption. However, the addition of NH 4 SCN may introduce hydrogen absorption rate fluctuations at high applied electrical potentials [ 50 ,  51 ]. Except for the electrochemical charging method, high pressure gas charging method is also applied for hydrogen charging purposes [ 52 ]. After hydrogen charging, the charged specimens are transferred for a slow strain rate tensile test. The typical strain rate of this test is around 1 × 10 –5 /s, because a fast strain rate allows little time for hydrogen diffusion, leading to the underestimation of hydrogen embrittlement risk [ 18 ]. Finally, the UTS and ductility loss due to hydrogen charging are measured for the subsequent analysis of hydrogen embrittlement risks. Although this method is straightforward and widely used in studying hydrogen embrittlement, the limitation of this method is apparent. Most importantly, the distribution of hydrogen in the charged sample is nonuniform. Because the driving force for hydrogen diffusion is the concentration gradient, the concentration of hydrogen is noticeably higher in the surface parts of the specimen, while that concentration is relatively low in the core interior of the specimen. Under the same total hydrogen content, this nonuniform distribution of hydrogen significantly increases the risk of hydrogen-induced brittle fracture at surface regions, while reducing the possibility of such failure within internal regions. This disparity may lead to misjudgment of the locations most susceptible to hydrogen embrittlement in the material. Additionally, the charged hydrogen tends to efflux into the atmosphere during specimen deformation, resulting in a significant reduction of the overall hydrogen content within the material compared to the initial value. This phenomenon may lead to the underestimation of hydrogen embrittlement risk for the material at a target hydrogen concentration. To compensate for this deficiency, the in-situ hydrogen charging method is gradually being adopted for hydrogen charging experiments [ 53 ].

Constant load test is widely applied by the automotive industry for evaluating the hydrogen embrittlement risk of high-strength steel [ 54 ,  55 ]. The specimen is immersed in an acid solution to facilitate the reaction between hydrogen ions and iron elements, thereby generating hydrogen, which provides the hydrogen resources. The fracture time and the applied load are measured for the hydrogen embrittlement risk evaluation. Four-point bending test is also widely adopted by industry due to its simple procedure, low equipment requirements, and rapid results, making it suitable for preliminary assessment of hydrogen embrittlement risk in materials.

In addition to the widely used hydrogen embrittlement assessment methods mentioned above, new evaluation techniques are also under development. The slow-strain-rate tensile test after austenitization and press quenching under controlled dew point has been applied to evaluate the hydrogen embrittlement risk of PHS [ 56 ]. Compared to the hydrogen precharge method, this new method allows for a more uniform distribution of hydrogen within the material and results in a hydrogen content that more closely reflects actual industrial production conditions.

sections.heading: Hydrogen embrittlement of quenching and partitioning (Q&P) steels
paragraphs: Quenching and partitioning (Q&P) steel is one of the 3rd generations of AHSS and has already been widely applied in the automotive industry for lightweight. One typical chemical composition of Q&P steel is Fe-0.3C-3Mn-1.5Si (wt.%). The microstructure of Q&P steel is featured by the retained austenite in addition to martensite and/or ferrite matrix. [ 57 ] The typical volume fraction of retained austenite ranges from 10 to 25%. As represented by the microstructure in Fig.  8 a. The general fabrication process is illustrated in Fig.  8 b. The austenitizing and quenching process aims to obtain adequate martensite; the subsequent partitioning aims to preserve austenite with proper mechanical stability. sections.heading: Hydrogen embrittlement of commercial Q&P steels
Hydrogen trap behavior and embrittlement mechanisms
paragraphs: In Q&P steels, retained austenite plays an important role in providing strain hardening via the TRIP effect [ 60 ,  61 – 62 ] and trapping hydrogen as non-diffusible one [ 63 ,  64 ]. Specifically, the austenite can trap more than 3 times hydrogen content over that in martensite matrix in a QP980 steel [ 65 ]. On the other side, the interface between austenite and martensite phase could play as crack initiation site and propagation paths for the hydrogen induced brittle fracture. Moreover, due to the complexity of the microstructure in Fig.  8 a, multiple defects, such as boundaries among martensite, ferrite, and austenite, martensite block boundaries, and carbides, also offer trapping ability. In this case, the martensite/ferrite, ferrite/austenite, and martensite/austenite boundaries primarily absorb reversible hydrogen and delay hydrogen diffusion, while the film austenite is a strong trap site for reversible hydrogen; in contrast, the blocky austenite, as a trap site for irreversible hydrogen, can not only limit the diffusivity of hydrogen but also increase hydrogen solubility [ 66 ]. With abundant trap sites and multiple phases in Q&P steel, the kinetics for the hydrogen evolution reaction can be effectively enhanced [ 66 ]. Besides, since the fresh martensite, which comes from the strain-induced martensitic transformation, is extremely vulnerable to hydrogen embrittlement, the austenite stability in the deformation process becomes critical. It is found that 20Mn-Si Q&P steel (Fe-0.2C-2.5Mn-1.5Si (wt.%)), a prolonged partition will lead to the increase of austenite stability by carbon partition, which could effectively enhance the hydrogen embrittlement resistance of that steel [ 61 ]. The influence of Mn segregation band in QP1180 has also been evaluated [ 67 ]. Because of the high dislocation density in the coarse martensite within the Mn band, this band is the origin of the cracking. The priority for the hydrogen trapping sites is as following: Mn band, retain austenite, PAGB, martensite block boundary, martensite, and ferrite [ 67 ].

With hydrogen, multiple mechanical properties of steel, like tensile yield stress, ultimate stress and bendability, are degraded [ 59 ]. A comparison work has been conducted among DP steel (Fe-0.09C-0.28Si-2.4Mn-0.03Al-0.04Nb-0.02Ti in wt.%), Q&P steel (Fe-0.2C-1.5Si-2.0Mn-0.03Al-0.04Nb-0.01Ti) and TWIP steel (Fe-0.6C-0.09Si-15.2Mn-1.46Al), which reports that hydrogen induced crack initiates at (i) martensite, (ii) martensite/ferrite interface, (iii) martensite/austenite interface, (iv) deformation twins [ 68 ]. Further investigation in QP980 indicates that the cracking mechanisms are dependent on hydrogen content, as illustrated in Fig.  9  [ 69 ]. Under a low hydrogen circumstance (0.64 ppm), the cracks will initiate at martensite and martensite/ferrite boundary but be blunt by ferrite, thus minorly impairing tensile properties; when a medium hydrogen (1.46 ppm) pre-charged into QP980, the hydrogen-induced cracks that nucleate at martensite/ferrite boundary will propagate through the HELP mechanism; if QP980 is saturated with hydrogen (above 3 ppm), the ferrite will be embrittled by transgranular cleavage along {110} slip plane by the HEDE mechanism. Fig. 9 Hydrogen-assisted fracture process and hydrogen embrittlement mechanism of QP980 under different hydrogen contents:  a  low hydrogen content;  b  middle hydrogen content;  c  high hydrogen content. Reprinted from [ 69 ] with permission. Copyright 2025 Elsevier

Both QP980 (Fe-0.19C-2.36Mn-1.69Si (wt.%)) and QP1180 (Fe-0.20C-2.39Mn-1.55Si (wt.%)) are widely used in the automotive industry. Comparison of them has also been made. Commercial QP1180 has much more complicated hydrogen trap sites than its counterpart QP980 [ 70 ]. On the one hand, the increased density of interfaces, including grain boundaries and phase boundaries, can simultaneously disperse hydrogen atoms and homogenize strains, ultimately minimizing stress concentration; on the other hand, the Mn element heterogeneously distributes in austenite and constructs chemical boundaries, where the Mn-poor (2 wt.%) and Mn-rich (6 wt.%) austenite regions react differently in deformation induced phase transformation and hydrogen releasing. Under such a situation, QP1180 behaves better when pre-charging with hydrogen [ 70 ]. However, another comparison work comes with an opposite phenomenon [ 62 ]. For the same strength grade, the specific alloy composition is in fact different. This situation could bring confusion and mislead when designing an anti-hydrogen strategy. Therefore, for Q&P steels, conclusions and implications should be carefully drawn and better from the aspect of microstructural design rather than correlating to the steel grade. During deformation of QP1180, the hard martensite-austenite island partitions more stress while the soft ferrite partitions more strains, whereas further stress-induced hydrogen accumulates at the martensite-austenite island in addition to previously trapped hydrogen; therefore, the martensite-austenite island can rapidly crack. Owing to more martensite-austenite islands components and connecting PAGB in QP1180, it demonstrates worse hydrogen embrittlement than the counterpart QP980. The discrepancy of hydrogen embrittlement risk evaluation results between these two research indicates the importance of controlling hydrogen distribution within steel during the deformation: in the former work, high density of interfaces prohibits the hydrogen local gathering through homogenizing strains, while the latter work lacks that mechanism due to the lack of high density interfaces, which results into the poor hydrogen embrittlement resistance of QP1180.

sections.heading: Effect of pre-straining on hydrogen embrittlement
paragraphs: Pre-strain can decipher the effect of deformed microstructures on hydrogen trapping and the origin of embrittlement. For instance, when pre-straining in the elastic stage using a constant load, the TDS curve demonstrates additional high-temperature peaks that are absent in the curves of the unstrained counterpart, which implies that austenite may take effect during loading [ 71 ]. The assertion has been proven by differential scanning calorimetry measurement, in which the decomposition of austenite has been observed at the same temperature [ 71 ]. In comparison, when pre-strained into the plastic stage, austenite partially transforms into fresh martensite, and the dislocation density increases in the matrix, which combinedly elevates the trap sites and decreases the effective diffusion coefficient [ 72 ]. But another points out that the increased defect density only increases the content of diffusible hydrogen rather than non-diffusible hydrogen in QP1180 [ 73 ].

With more trap sites after pre-strain, the HEDE mechanism becomes predominant, in contrast to the hydrogen-enhanced micro void coalescence in non-pre-strained QP1180 [ 58 ]. Specifically, hydrogen-induced microcracks initiate readily in transformed martensite after pre-strain. When the pre-strain amount is adequate, the ferrite can still blunt crack propagation; when the pre-strain is large, hydrogen trapped by high-density dislocations will cause transgranular cracks in distorted ferrite [ 58 ]. For fast prediction of hydrogen susceptibility, researchers have constructed the relationship among pre-strain amount, critical hydrogen content, and critical fracture stress in QP1180, as shown in Fig.  10  [ 74 ]. Figure  10  indicates that both hydrogen content and the pre-strain contribute to the hydrogen induced fracture, and the effect of pre-strain on the critical fracture stress of the material gradually increases with increasing hydrogen content. Fig. 10 Relationship among pre-strain amount, critical hydrogen content, and critical fracture stress. Reprinted from [ 74 ] with permission. Copyright 2023 Elsevier

sections.heading: Welding effect on hydrogen embrittlement
paragraphs: Welding processing is usually applied in the automotive industry, especially for fabricating components made of Q&P steels. To address the issue of hydrogen-sensitive heat-affected zone (HAZ), the QP980 has been subjected to a laser in situ post-weld heat treatment process [ 75 ]. After such heat treatment, carbides can precipitate in the martensite matrix of the intercritical HAZ and enhance its hydrogen resistance, finally transferring the hydrogen fracture to the base material zone [ 75 ].

After friction stir welding (FSW) of QP980, the weld joint remains in a high residual stress state, and even hydrogen pre-charging can cause cracks to appear successively in intercritical HAZ, base materials zone, and stirred zone, with increasing hydrogen content as displayed in Fig.  11  [ 76 ]. In these areas, intergranular cracks along martensite/ferrite boundaries and transgranular cracks inner martensite are observed in the former two zones, while the latter zone predominantly suffers trans martensite cracks [ 76 ]. Fig. 11 The macrostructure of FSW joints of QP980 steel charged for  a  0 h,  b  1 h,  c  2 h,  d  4 h,  e  8 h, and  f  16 h. Reprinted from [ 76 ] with permission. Copyright 2021 Elsevier

sections.heading: Hydrogen embrittlement related processing improvement and technology promotion
Additional treatment
paragraphs: To further improve the hydrogen embrittlement of Q&P steels, processing design has been explored by incorporating additional treatment. For example, in QP1180 with ~ 3 wt.% Mn, segregation band can form during solidification and be hardly eliminated by thermomechanical processing, so that it jeopardizes the mechanical property after hydrogen pre-charging [ 67 ]. To tackle this problem, a two-pass fast tempering (infrared heating (> 100 °C/s) to 400 °C, followed by holding for 2 min and then quenching in water) has been conducted after Q&P treatment (Q&P&TT), after which the coarse combined martensite island in the Mn band transforms into an isolated martensite island, ferrite, and austenite as present in Fig.  12 ; as a result, the hydrogen-induced crack nucleation shifts from the Mn band to the steel surface [ 77 ]. Fig. 12 a  Q&P and  b  Q&P&TT processed. Reproduced from [ 77 ] with permission. Copyright 2024 Elsevier

There are abundant works utilizing tempering, substituting partitioning as Q&T treatment [ 78 ,  79 ,  80 – 81 ] and supplementing as Q-P-T treatment [ 82 ,  83 – 84 ]. For steel with the chemical composition of Fe-0.4C-1.5Mn-1.5Si, in both Q&P (austenitized at 860 °C or 950 °C for 5 min, then immersed in molten salt at 240 °C for 15 s, then transferred to another molten bath with 420 °C for 30 s, finally water quench) and Q&T (austenitized at 860 °C or 950 °C for 5 min, then tempered at 420 °C for 120 s) heat treatment, its hydrogen resistance benefits from refined microstructure; however, the steel after Q&T treatment exhibits more serious hydrogen embrittlement than the Q&P counterpart, owing to a lack of stable austenite, as shown in Fig.  13 a, b [ 63 ]. In comparison, for steels after Q-P-T treatment, ε-carbides form during tempering and can trap hydrogen atoms (Fig.  13 c, d) [ 85 ]. Nevertheless, it is reported that for Q&T treatment and various Q&P treatments, the product steels manifest nearly no hydrogen embrittlement during corrosion tests and Zn electroplating without the usage of recombination poison; in addition, the negative influence of hydrogen formed during Zn electroplating can be limited by using proper electrolytes and electrical parameters [ 86 ]. These findings indicated the relationship between the recombination poison, electrolytes and hydrogen embrittlement of Q&T/Q&P steels needs further investigation. Moreover, the intercritical temperature range has been used to tailor microstructure with ferrite and refined microstructure in Q&P steels, namely IAQ&P. There are two routes for the IAQ step. First, using direct heating through intercritical annealing instead of traditional austenitizing produces a significant amount of ferrite. This process also helps to partition more manganese and carbon into the blocky and film-like austenite, respectively. As a result, the stability of the austenite is improved, allowing the soft ferrite to withstand strain during deformation. Additionally, the formation of ferrite during intercritical annealing greatly refines the microstructure after quenching, effectively disrupting the continuity of PAGB [ 87 ]. Another work induces pre-quenching before IAQ&P and further refines the microstructure, as well as creating more trap sites [ 88 ]. Another method for IAQ is to heat the material to the austenitizing temperature, then gradually cool it down to the intercritical temperature before quenching. However, it seems that IAQ&P in this route cannot remarkably improve hydrogen resistance, compared with Q&P and Q-P-T [ 64 ,  89 ]. The inferior property after IAQ&P should be attributed to the large blocky austenite [ 89 ]. Nonetheless, the potential for IAQ&P deserves further exploitation.

sections.heading: Q&P-treated steels
paragraphs: Q&P processing has also been promoted to other alloy systems to fabricate high-performance materials. For example, 2 GPa grade martensitic steels can be obtained by the Q&P process [ 90 ]. Alloying by Si and Al has been compared, and the effect of the partitioning process has been appraised. Compared with that merely quenched, the Si-containing steel undergoes Q&P, possesses a higher fraction of austenite and accordingly hinders hydrogen infusion and accumulation, thereupon behaving better with hydrogen pre-charging; furthermore, the Al-containing Q&P steel show thicker filmy austenite which absorbs more hydrogen atoms, while Al element in martensite matrix drives hydrogen diffusion to austenite, further declining the hydrogen diffusivity and hydrogen content. The latter phenomenon is validated by density functional theory calculations, saying that Si increases the solubility of hydrogen in martensite than Al (formation energy of hydrogen in Si containing Fe is −1.44 eV and in Al containing Fe is −0.65 eV)[ 90 ].

Q&P processing makes marvelous improvements in press hardened steels (PHS). After Q&P treatment, fine and stable austenite can be formed in PHS, which reduces hydrogen diffusion and limits hydrogen content; such stable austenite can transform the fracture mechanism from intergranular and quasi-cleavage cracks dominant into dimple dominant [ 91 ]. Meanwhile, it is found that a higher partitioning temperature is also helpful in resisting hydrogen in PHS1500 [ 92 ]. Although the hydrogen trapping behavior demonstrates limited improvement, the mechanical response of the composition phases indeed alters. Specifically, the mechanical stability of austenite decreases slightly and provides the TRIP effect, while the martensite matrix contains fewer dislocations and carbon content, in which case it suffers a much lower flow stress and earns better intrinsic fracture toughness as well as hydrogen resistance [ 92 ].

sections.heading: Unsolved problems and possible outlook of hydrogen embrittlement of Q&P steel
paragraphs: Although the Q&P has been extensively used in industries, the fundamental investigation on hydrogen embrittlement still lacks. For example, if the higher strength grade QP1500 is promoted to market, hydrogen embrittlement will be a major challenge, while the relevant studies have not been conducted. There are many similar problems in the research on hydrogen embrittlement of Q&P steels. In this section, several urgent issues are noted.

For the same strength grade, the specific alloy composition is in fact different, as listed in Table  1 . This situation could bring confusion and mislead when designing an anti-hydrogen strategy. Therefore, for Q&P steels, conclusions and implications should be carefully drawn and better from the aspect of microstructural design rather than correlating to the steel grade. Moreover, in most studies, slow strain rate tensile tests (SSRT) are the primary assessment technique. To comprehensively evaluate hydrogen sensitivity and simulate specific service conditions, diversified assessment techniques are recommended to be conducted. For example, deep-drawn cups (Fig.  15 a) with various drawing ratios have been immersed in and sprayed by salty water to evaluate the hydrogen embrittlement, in addition to SSRT in Q&P steel [ 21 ]. This combined method can help better understand the underlying mechanism that, when plastic deformation and residual stress remain comparable, the larger ferrite faction and the topological distribution that disrupts PAGB and separates martensite packets are critical [ 21 ]. The U-bend tests (Fig.  15 b) are also complementary for simulating complex stress states [ 93 ]. The hydrogen resistance of DP1180 and QP1180 has been compared by U-bend tests [ 94 ]. It is found, for both materials, that hydrogen embrittlement only happens near the bending limit and by micro-voids/microcracks from severe plastic deformation; associated with better plasticity, QP1180 demonstrates a greater resistance thanks to a smaller plastic strain at the smallest bend radius, compared with DP1180 [ 94 ]. The hydrogen fracture initiation and early fracture propagation was by the mechanisms designated as hydrogen fracture due to hydrogen enhanced microvoid coalescence. Late-stage hydrogen fracture growth was by quasi-cleavage for DP1180 and intergranular fracture for QP1180. Furthermore, tensile tests under different strain rates can help understand scenarios such as forming and a car crash. In an Nb-containing Q&P steel, the microstructure is tailored with a refined martensite matrix, NbC precipitation, and more retained austenite, which results in a higher hydrogen content and a higher desorption temperature because of re-trapping by NbC [ 95 ]. In this Q&P steel, the excessive retained austenite jeopardizes its hydrogen resistance under a slow strain rate, while the hydrogen embrittlement is largely suppressed under a high strain rate due to constrained hydrogen diffusion and limited TRIP effect which is caused by adiabatic heating [ 95 ,  96 ]. In certain cases, comprehensive techniques are desired, and multiple factors are also necessary for constructing a performance prediction system. As aforementioned, changing pre-strain by constant load tests can obtain the relationship among pre-strain amount, critical hydrogen content, and critical fracture stress [ 74 ]. This method can be promoted to dominant factors such as boundary density and austenite fraction, and so on.

sections.heading: Novel microstructure design
paragraphs: Novel microstructural design strategies have been proposed to obtain prominent mechanical properties in Q&P steels under non-hydrogen circumstances. How these strategies fight against hydrogen embrittlement deserves future investigations.

For example, a threefold heterogeneous and bimodal microstructure can be obtained by two-cycle IAQ&P treatment. During the 2nd IAQ&P, recrystallization of 1st martensite, austenite reversion, and growth of 1st ferrite occur simultaneously, obtaining a microstructure with soft coarse ferrite surrounded by hard fine martensite and austenite. Such heterogeneity causes significant dislocation forest strengthening and hetero-deformation-induced strengthening by increased density of geometrically necessary dislocations [ 97 ]. Moreover, chemical patterning has been proven to be a good strategy to improve tensile properties [ 98 ,  99 – 100 ]. Due to precipitation of traditional Q&P treatment, the carbon is largely consumed by carbides. To address this, fast austenitizing has been conducted, during which the Mn-rich austenite can partition more C due to the interaction between Mn and C, and finally lead to a nanosized alternating austenite/martensite morphology, resulting in prominent property than traditional Q&P [ 101 ]. Besides, additive manufacturing can make a great difference. In a laser powder bed fusion manufacturing (LPBF), a Q&T steel has been fabricated with cyclic quenching after solidification and an extra tempering after printing; the most remarkable effect by LPBF is that the chemical distribution is quite homogeneous and no segregation band occurs even with 10 wt.% Mn; the final tempering minimizes the residual stress of the as-printed steel and reverses the residual stress in austenite, finally contributing to exceptional mechanical performance [ 102 ].

sections.heading: Welding of dissimilar plates
paragraphs: The assessment and amelioration of hydrogen embrittlement in the weld joint of Q&P and another dissimilar plate is an essential yet difficult field. For instance, the retained austenite evolution and the weakness point have been determined in a laser butt welding of dissimilar QP980 and B1500HS [ 103 ]. However, the hydrogen susceptibility of the weld joint has not been revealed. QP980 has also been resistance spot welded with a TWIP1000 [ 104 ] and DP600 [ 105 ], respectively. Effects of welding parameters are compared to optimize shear strength, and the microstructural evolutions of both plates have been characterized. In future research, the database of the response from dissimilar joints to hydrogen is desired because it can provide more guidance for process optimization and steel grade selection.

sections.heading: Hydrogen embrittlement of medium Mn steels (MMS)
paragraphs: Medium Mn steels (MMS) are one of the 3rd generations of AHSS, which contain Mn content in the range of 3–12 wt.%, and one typical carbon content is in the range of 0.1–0.5 wt.%. The strength level of MMS typically ranges from 900 to 1600 MPa. The microstructure of MMS is characterized by martensite, ferrite, and metastable austenite [ 57 ,  106 ]. Through manipulating chemical compositions and thermomechanical processes, outstanding mechanical properties, such as strength-ductility product exceeding 60 GPa·% [ 107 ,  108 – 109 ], can be achieved, thus attracting enormous interest in academia and industry. On the other hand, high-strength MMS usually suffers from hydrogen embrittlement [ 110 ], which intrigues researchers in exploiting underlying mechanisms and corresponding solutions in the past decade.

sections.heading: Traditional intercritical annealing
paragraphs: Intercritical annealing refers to heating MMS between A c1  and A c3   [ 111 ], serving various purposes, such as alleviating residual stress, softening in before subsequent deformation, facilitating austenite reversion, and manipulating element distribution [ 112 ,  113 – 114 ]. Traditionally, batch annealing is conducted on MMS for hours. For example, conducting intercritical annealing for a long duration on a cold-rolled MMS alters the morphology largely and leads to superior mechanical properties regardless of hydrogen content, compared with the prior hot-rolled counterpart, though they show similar austenite phase fraction and element partition because of equilibrium [ 115 ]. The temperature of intercritical annealing imposes multiple influences and has triggered arguments. It is reported that higher temperature leads to higher austenite fraction and lower C and Mn partition, resulting in reduced mechanical stability of austenite (Fig.  16 a) and thus more deformation-induced martensite that is susceptible to hydrogen [ 116 ]. On the other hand, increasing intercritical annealing temperature can adversely enhance Mn partitioning and contribute to austenite stability [ 117 ], hence improve hydrogen resistance despite elevated hydrogen content (Fig.  16 b). Fig. 16 Effect of intercritical annealing temperature.  a  Austenite fraction-intercritical annealing temperature curves [ 116 ].  b  Elongation loss-retained austenite fraction curves [ 117 ]. Reproduced from [ 116 ,  117 ] with permission. Copyright 2019 Elsevier

Diffrent from the dispute on temperature, works on intercritical annealing duration (IAD) usually reach a consensus that the IAD usually monotonically influences hydrogen sensitivity. By prolonging annealing, the austenite grains and fractions grow while the C/Mn partitions decrease, prompting profuse TRIP effect (Fig.  17 a, b) and deteriorating hydrogen resistance [ 118 ,  119 ]. In another work [ 120 ], lamellar δ-ferrite has been incorporated into the microstructure to investigate its role in influencing hydrogen embrittlement by the addition of Si. The Si addition narrows the austenite phase zone and reduces austenite fraction, while for each steel grade, longer intercritical annealing duration reduces austenite stability and undermines mechanical properties with hydrogen in Fig.  17 c. sections.heading: Novel intercritical annealing
paragraphs: As IAD plays an important and intriguing role in MMS, it provokes advancement in processing and creates nonequilibrium microstructures by well-tuning the duration. A novel intercritical annealing technique, named short-duration annealing or flash annealing, has thus been invented [ 121 ,  122 ]. Exceptional mechanical properties of MMS with chemical boundary engineering can be obtained by flash annealing [ 123 ]. Certainly, the effectiveness of such novel processing has also been verified in alleviating hydrogen embrittlement. For example, immediate heating for only 90 s generates a nano-twinned microstructure in a medium Mn Hadfield steel, where dislocation cross-slip and storage are inhibited while strain homogeneity is stimulated by fine twinning, thus resisting hydrogen embrittlement [ 124 ]. For industrially hot-rolled and batch annealed MMS, austenite in one single prior austenite grain (PAG) exhibits the same orientation, which results in strain localization at austenite-ferrite interfaces where hydrogen-induced cracks occur, as displayed in Fig.  18 a–c; while after conducting a small amount of cold-rolling and short-duration intercritical annealing, the austenite stability is enhanced and dislocation cells in ferrite can strongly trap hydrogen as present in Fig.  18 d–f [ 125 ]. Moreover, inspired by the nonequilibrium frozen effect by short-duration intercritical annealing, a chemical heterogeneity has been proposed to fight hydrogen embrittlement [ 126 ], which will be reviewed later. sections.heading: Cold, hot, and warm treatment
paragraphs: Cold forming is a common forming technique for parts; however, cold deformation usually induces more serious hydrogen embrittlement [ 127 ,  128 ]. With elevated cold deformation by pre-straining, the austenite transforms into martensite, and the dislocation density increases. As a result, the hydrogen diffusion can be significantly enhanced, and more diffusible hydrogen enters MMS. In this case, hydrogen atoms embrittle the boundaries between pre-introduced martensite and dislocated ferrite [ 127 ].

Hot treatment has an effect akin to cold deformation. For example, granular morphology can be obtained by traditional cold-rolling and intercritical annealing, which absorbs less hydrogen and resists embrittlement; while adding an austenitizing step before annealing results in heterogeneous morphology with lamellar and granular grains, which absorbs much more hydrogen and deteriorates properties [ 129 ]. Hot-rolling processing can lead to a similar phenomenon. The more reduction during hot-rolling, the higher austenite fraction and the inferior mechanical stability, which is detrimental to hydrogen resistance; while decreasing the reduction of hot-rolling results in a steric coarse ferrite network and triggers the HELP mechanism instead of the HEDE mechanism [ 130 ].

Despite cold and hot treatments, a novel processing technique, namely warm treatment with deformation under intercritical temperatures, has emerged to fabricate MMS with exceptional mechanical properties [ 7 ,  8 ,  131 ]. The warm-rolling can be incorporated with short-duration intercritical annealing to optimize hydrogen resistance [ 132 ], attributing to the elimination of PAGB by warm-rolling. Furthermore, the morphology tailored by warm-rolling introduces topological benefits. In other words, elongated grains contribute to less vulnerability to hydrogen. Typically, when loading along rolling direction, the transvers propagation of hydrogen-induced cracks can either consume vast energy by tear mechanism [ 133 ] (Fig.  19 a), or be frequently deflected to generate delamination and reduce stress triaxiality [ 133 ,  134 ,  135 – 136 ] (Fig.  19 c, d). sections.heading: Other techniques
paragraphs: Recently, researchers tried to sophisticatedly tune the microstructure by an additional tempering. For instance, adding a tempering process after intercritical annealing results in decomposition of austenite and formation of cementite, which improves anti-hydrogen properties albeit to different hydrogen trapping behavior [ 137 ]. In comparison, the temperature of quenching, after annealing and before tempering, has been also investigated [ 138 ]. It is found that by reducing the quenching temperature after annealing, a refined microstructure with stable filmy austenite can be observed [ 138 ].

Additionally, some works focus on resorting properties degraded by hydrogen. It is reported that conventional annealing at 250 ℃ can only resort partially the mechanical properties, while electric pulsed treatment fully resorts the tensile performance [ 139 ]. Moreover, this treatment can be easily incorporated with baking and galvanization.

sections.heading: Welding processing and hydrogen embrittlement
paragraphs: Welding of MMS is an important research field and garners increasing attention in the perspective of hydrogen embrittlement. In a gas metal arc welding (GMAW) study, the fracture point transits from weld materials to heat affected zone (HAZ), in both Ti-free joint and Ti-containing joint, owing to higher hydrogen content in HAZ [ 140 ]. Furthermore, for the Ti-containing joint, it has a much higher hydrogen content compared with that in the Ti-free counterpart, because of lacking austenite [ 140 ].

The friction stir welding (FSW) of MMS has also been investigated. Grain refinement and high-density dislocations are achieved in both δ-ferrite band and α-ferrite/austenite band after FSW [ 141 ]. However, due to the elevated stress concentration at α-ferrite/austenite interfaces and at δ-ferrite boundaries, the MMS after FSW demonstrates worse hydrogen embrittlement in Fig.  20 a [ 141 ]. To address this problem, another work employs an additional intercritical annealing after FSW [ 142 ]. By intercritical annealing, fine reverted austenite grains are introduced at PAG, packet and block boundaries, which can effectively absorb hydrogen and minimize the diffusivity of hydrogen (Fig.  20 b), thereby optimizing hydrogen resistance [ 142 ]. Although a higher temperature leads to a more remarkable decrease in hydrogen content, low temperature annealing brings benefits via stabilized austenite [ 142 ]. Fig. 20 a  Tensile properties of base materials and FSW joint without/with hydrogen.  b  Hydrogen diffusivity evaluation by permeation test of MMS subjected to FSW and subsequent annealing. Reproduced from [ 141 ,  142 ] with permission. Copyright 2025 and Copyright 2024 Elsevier

Mn can be readily segregated and detrimental to mechanical properties, including hydrogen embrittlement [ 67 ,  77 ,  143 ]; therefore, the Mn evolution during welding should have significant influence on hydrogen susceptibility. However, there is a scarcity of comprehensive research examining the welding-induced Mn segregation and resultant hydrogen embrittlement resistance of MMS.

sections.heading: Alloying/aging on hydrogen embrittlement
paragraphs: Aging is usually conducted to gain precipitation/dispersion strengthening in MMS [ 144 ,  145 – 146 ]. There is abundant research exploiting the merits of precipitations/carbides in enhancing hydrogen resistance. In an early study, Nb, Ti and V additions successfully generate various carbides in MMS, yet they have a trivial effect on hydrogen embrittlement, because these carbides are primarily precipitate in ferrite whereas hydrogen-induced cracks dominantly occur in austenite [ 147 ]. It is anticipated that precipitation in austenite would make a great difference. To this end, Cu has been added into a MMS and aged to form Cu-rich precipitates in austenite accompanying NiAl in ferrite [ 148 ]. It is reported that the strategy of co-precipitation reduces mechanical contrast between austenite and ferrite, and minimize strain transfer at phase boundaries, ultimately lessening hydrogen sensitivity [ 148 ]. Besides, further investigation found that Nb-carbides has a variable effect on hydrogen embrittlement, depending on the strain rates [ 149 ]. It is interesting that the incoherent Nb-carbides can only trap hydrogen under higher rates such as 5 × 10 –5  s −1  [ 149 ].

Alloying may have beneficial effects in addition to precipitations. For instance, Nb/Mo addition can refine grains, precipitate carbides and stabilize austenite to minimize diffusible hydrogen [ 150 ]. However, inadequate simultaneous addition of Nb and Mo could result in large blocky austenite, in contrast to filmy austenite at PAGB, and thereafter undermines the beneficial effects [ 151 ]. Besides, element segregation also plays a vital role. It is proven that Mn segregation at PAGB causes disastrous hydrogen embrittlement while a slight addition of B can cause occupation at PAGB, strengthening boundary bonding and repulsing hydrogen accumulation [ 143 ].

In addition, incorporation of warm-rolling and tempering in a Ni-containing MMS can serve multiple functions, contributing to hydrogen resistance [ 152 ]. Heterogeneous Ni-containing nano precipitates and self-stabilized austenite can optimize the deformation compatibility and reduce plasticity instability; moreover, precipitates act as hydrogen trap sites [ 152 ].

sections.heading: Austenite engineering and hydrogen embrittlement
paragraphs: Austenite is the most noteworthy feature of MMS, because of the merit of TRIP effect from it. And austenite also plays an essential role in most research on hydrogen of MMS, referred to as Austenite Engineering. The effect of austenite originates from its high solubility of hydrogen and transformation into martensite [ 153 ], and can be investigated in three aspects: fraction, topology and stability.

As regarded as a composition phase in traditional intercritical annealing under different temperatures, the austenite exhibits largely different volume fractions. At a high temperature, the austenite is the dominant phase and forms a steric network, namely having a high topological percolation for hydrogen transportation [ 42 ]. In this case, hydrogen has to be absorbed by austenite and permeate into steel interior. As a result, hydrogen atoms mostly reside in austenite and initiate cracking at fresh martensite under the HEDE mechanism. In contrast, hydrogen atoms predominantly penetrate the topologically percolated ferrite network and commence cracking at dislocation tangles in ferrite with the help of the HELP mechanism [ 42 ]. In fact, the topologic percolation of austenite can not only be tailored by its volume fraction, but also by its morphology. When conducting prior austenitizing under high and low temperature, lamellar and granular morphology are obtained, respectively [ 154 ]. As for the lamellar austenite, it has a higher percolation because of none recrystallization. Such interconnective austenite subsequently blocks hydrogen transportation and reduces the hydrogen content, thereby resisting hydrogen embrittlement [ 154 ].

When the austenite has a fraction and morphology insufficient to become the matrix phase, it usually serves as strong hydrogen trap sites for its high desorption energy [ 155 ,  156 – 157 ]. For example, tempering and intercritical annealing are usually conducted to obtain a small fraction of austenite to trap diffusible hydrogen and prevent hydrogen cracking [ 138 ,  142 ]. Large fraction of austenite trap site can also be obtained by tuning parameters of intercritical annealing [ 158 ]. Given comparable kinetics of martensitic transformation, the MMS with a longer Luders band demonstrates more serious embrittlement after hydrogen pre-charging; it should be attributed to the faster transformation and the higher flow stress in Luders band [ 158 ].

Since most studies make use of the TRIP effect from metastable austenite, the concomitant austenite stability becomes a significant factor determining hydrogen susceptibility. Generally, the inferior of the mechanical stability, the severer the hydrogen embrittlement [ 159 ]. To address this issue and make the best of the TRIP effect, an elongated banded morphology, made by warm-rolling, is successfully employed to get in the way of propagation of hydrogen-induced cracks [ 136 ]. Other solutions mainly emphasize increasing the mechanical stability of austenite, which inevitably sacrifices work hardening [ 116 ,  118 ]. More solutions without the expense of the TRIP effect are desired. Therefore, a heterogeneous stability of austenite is proposed, namely the martensitic transformation progresses at a specific order. In the warm-rolled MMS, large and blocky austenite band transforms first while the filmy austenite can still blunt crack propagation [ 136 ]. Such random-heterogeneous stability in grain scale is also achieved in MMS as illustrated in Fig.  21 a [ 126 ]. By conducting flash annealing, the none-equilibrium state of Mn distribution can be preserved at room temperature, contributing to various stability of austenite at grain interior; the hydrogen-induced cracks, nucleating at Mn-poor region, can be subsequently arrested by un-transformed Mn-rich austenite region, during crack propagation [ 126 ]. In contrast, an ordered-heterogenous stability of austenite is also realized in grain scale as depicted in Fig.  21 b, c [ 160 ,  161 ]. A so-called core–shell model substantially emphasizes the characteristics. Given that the austenite traps the majority of hydrogen, the hydrogen-induced cracks mostly arise from the Mn-poor cores and can be ineluctably blocked by the Mn-rich shell; In addition, due to the isolation by the shell, the stress concentration between fresh martensite and ferrite, in most other cases, can be avoided, so that cracks at martensite/ferrite boundaries are minimized [ 160 ,  161 ]. sections.heading: Manufacturing PHS
paragraphs: Boron steels are the most widely used PHS in the automotive industry, and currently 22MnB5 steel is the most popular steel among these boron steels [ 162 ]. Two major hot stamping methods are applied: direct and indirect hot stamping. The processes of these two methods are shown in Fig.  22 . For direct hot stamping, the plate of raw material is heated up for austenitization, then the plate is transferred for the subsequent forming and quenching by the cooling mold. The indirect forming method includes an extra cold pre-forming step before the austenitization step. Before the hot stamping, the raw material of 22MnB5 consists of a ferrite and pearlite mixture with a maximum tensile stress of roughly 600 MPa. After the hot stamping process, the microstructure of the steel completely transforms to a full martensitic structure. The strength of this material is boosted to 1500 MPa due to the different microstructure. It needs to be pointed out that the cooling rate of the steel plate is critical for the formation of a full martensitic microstructure, because the cooling rate less than 27 K/s leads to the formation of extra austenite bainite and ferrite [ 9 ], which may affect the mechanical properties of the material. The importance of the cooling rate on the formation of a full martensitic microstructure explains the population of boron steels in PHS. The addition of the boron element effectively enhances the hardenability of steel. Boron preferentially segregates at austenite grain boundaries when the steel plate is in the austenitization state. Then, during the cooling stage, boron effectively reduces the grain boundary energy and thereby restricts the formation of softer phases like bainite, ferrite, and pearlite. However, the boron enhancement on steel hardenability is influenced by multiple factors. Boron must be in its atomic form to function properly. If boron is in its oxide, carbide, or nitride state, its effect on hardenability enhancement will be lost. Therefore, extra titanium, aluminum, and zirconium are added to steel to consume the harmful nitrogen. Fig. 22 a  Direct and  b  indirect hot stamping process of manufacturing PHS. Reprinted from [ 9 ] with permission. Copyright 2010 Elsevier

sections.heading: Microstructure and related hydrogen embrittlement of PHS
paragraphs: Prior austenite grain boundary (PAGB) is another susceptible site for hydrogen embrittlement of PHS. Hydrogen accumulates on PAGB during the deformation process because the slip of dislocations transports the adjacent hydrogen to PAGB. HMT successfully proves this accumulation of hydrogen on PAGB under tensile stress-induced deformation (Fig.  26 ). It is clear that hydrogen accumulates on the PAGB according to the comparison between Fig.  26 a, b. Takai et al. [ 164 ] designed a delicate experiment to prove that the segregation of hydrogen at PAGB during the deformation is the major cause of brittle fracture of PHS. The PHS specimens are divided into several groups. For the first group, the specimen is hydrogen-charged and stored in a −196 °C environment to prevent the diffusion of hydrogen. Then, the uniaxial tensile test was conducted on this specimen at −196 °C. The specimen exhibits typical ductile fracture behavior with a relatively long segment of non-uniform deformation (Fig.  27 b). The second group of materials is hydrogen charged and preloaded at several different stresses before it is unloaded and stored in low low-temperature environment (−196 °C), then the uniaxial tensile test has been conducted on these specimens at −196 °C (Fig.  27 a, b). All specimens show noticeable degradation in ductility when compared to group one, and this degradation becomes more profound with the increase of preload stress (Fig.  27 c). This result provides solid evidence that the hydrogen segregation at PAGB induces the brittle intergranular fracture of PHS. Fig. 26 a  SEM images of the specimen after applying tensile stress of 300 MPa and HMT.  b  EBSD mapping of the same area as ( a ). Reprinted from [ 165 ] with permission. Copyright 2020 Elsevier Fig. 27 Uniaxial tensile test results of  a ,  b  preloaded and  b  common tested specimens with and without hydrogen charge.  c  The relationship between ductility loss and the stress of preloading. Reprinted from [ 164 ] with permission. Copyright 2023 Elsevier

During the quenching step of heat treatment of PHS, the fast cooling rate leaves a noticeably high micro-scale residual stress inside the material. Mitigating the internal stress of ultra-high stress of PHS also effectively enhances its hydrogen embrittlement resistance. Luo et al. [ 22 ] has demonstrated that even using as low as 90 °C tempering could significantly relief the internal stress within the martensite matrix of the high strength PHS, which has been shown in Fig.  28 . It has been shown that the residual stress within the as quenched PHS is noticeably high (Fig.  28 b1, b2), and the maximum strain is as large as 0.48%. For tempered material, that strain is significantly smaller due to the relaxation effect from the tempering. The maximum strain is only 0.08% for the tempered PHS. This dramatically changed residual stress largely affects the hydrogen embrittlement resistance of high-strength steel. The mechanical performance of both hydrogen-charged and hydrogen-free specimens is shown in Fig.  29 . While the tensile properties of both as-quenched and tempered PHS show little difference (Fig.  29 a), their hydrogen embrittlement resistance is quite different (Fig.  29 b). The tensile properties of 90 °C tempered PHS are little affected by hydrogen. Without any addition of extra elements or changing of manufacturing process, this work demonstrates that only low temperature tempering could significantly enhance the hydrogen embrittlement resistance of ultra-high strength PHS, providing a material design strategy for mitigating the hydrogen embrittlement resistance of high strength PHS. sections.heading: PHS Surface structure and hydrogen embrittlement
paragraphs: To date, AlSi coating is the only widely commercially available coating technology for PHS worldwide, due to its excellent high temperature tolerance and great printability, and cost-efficiency [ 166 ]. ArcelorMittal filed a patent for this technology in 1999, and it was first commercially implemented in 2007 [ 162 ]. Ever since the commercialization of this technology, the production of PHS with AlSi coating has been booming [ 167 ,  168 ]. Reputable companies worldwide, such as Pasco and Baosteel, also hold numerous patents related to this technology [ 169 ,  170 ].

The hot dipping method has been applied to attach AlSi precoating on the surface of PHS in annealed state (Fig.  30 a). The dipping temperature is typically around 675 °C, and the chemical composition of the Al alloy bath is approximately 90% (wt.%) Al, with small amounts of Si and Fe. Gas jet wiping technique has been applied to control the thickness of precoating [ 162 ]. The purpose of adding Si into Al alloy bath is to form Si contained inhibition layer at the precoating and steel substrate interface, preventing the rapid diffusion of Al into steel substrate to form brittle intermetallics, like Fe 2 Al 5 , in the hot dipping step. The microstructure of AlSi precoating after hot dipping is shown in Fig.  30 . Fig. 30 a  Schematic for hot dipping method to make AlSi precoating.  b  The SEM image of AlSi precoating

After the addition of precoating, the steel sheets are transferred to furnace for austenitization. Considering the low melting temperature of Al (660 °C) and high furnace temperature (typically above 900 °C), the precoating melts in the initial stage of austenitization. Intense interdiffusion occurs between precoating and steel substrate [ 171 ]. After the austenitization and subsequent press and quenching, multi-layer surface structures have formed on the surface of PHS (Fig.  31 ). It is interesting to notice there are numerous Kirkendall voids forming on the prior precoating-steel interface, indicating the unbalanced and intense interdiffusion between precoating and steel substrate. Fig. 31 Surface structure of AlSi-coated 22MnB5 after austenitization and subsequent quenching

Zn coating, also known as galvanized (GI) and galvannealed (GA) coating, is also applied to PHS to provide cathodic corrosion protection. In corrosive environments, the coating itself will sacrificially corrode to protect the steel substrate from corrosion. The method of applying zinc coating onto steel substrates is similar to that of AlSi coating, both utilizing hot-dipping techniques. The zinc alloy bath consists of nearly pure Zn with an extra 0.2 wt.% Al, and the dipping temperature is around 460 °C. Then, the zinc-coated sheet cools to room temperature under ambient conditions.

The microstructure of GI precoating consists of a 10–20 μm pure zinc layer and a several-micron-thick intermetallic (Fe 2 Al 5 Zn) layer. Then the precoated sheets are transferred to the furnace for the subsequent austenitization. During the austenitization, the melted liquid state zinc and the surface oxides (ZnO) evaporate intensively, resulting in the noticeable thickness reduction during the austenitization step. This thickness reduction has not been observed in the AlSi coating. After austenitization, due to the interdiffusion between coating and steel substrate, only Г-ZnFe intermetallic and α-Fe(Zn) interdiffusion layer remain on the surface structure of zinc coated PHS. It needs to be mentioned that Г-ZnFe intermetallic provides the most effective cathodic corrosion protection, therefore, how to persevere more fraction of Г-ZnFe in the surface structure after austenitization is of great importance for the study of zinc coating.

Although zinc coating effectively protects PHS from oxidation, liquid metal embrittlement (LME) induced by melting zinc severely limits its industrial application. During the austenitization and the subsequent press step, the pure zinc layer in the zinc precoating melts due to the high furnace temperature. These liquids penetrate the steel substrate through cracks or grain boundaries under hot deformations, then weaken the materials by inducing embrittlement and generating cracks along grain boundaries. How to mitigate LME is the focus of the research on zinc coating of PHS.

Except for the two prevailing coating systems mentioned, other novel coating systems are also under development to protect PHS from oxidation. Dual Zn-Al layer coating has been designed by Lupp et al. [ 172 ] The hot dipping method is applied to attach precoating on the surface of as-annealed state steel sheet. The first layer of the precoating is formed through dipping in an Al alloy bath containing 10 wt.% Si, while the second layer is formed by dipping in Zn alloy bath containing 1 wt.% Al. A phosphating step is required for the precoating before the subsequent austenitization step. During the austenitization, interdiffusion occurs among the Zn, AlSi, and the steel substrate. The detailed phase constitutions of this novel coating system are still unclear and under investigation. Owing to the presence of AlSi layer, LME is largely inhibited. The phosphating step results in the formation of Zn 3 (PO 4 ) 2 H 2 O, which effectively suppresses the evaporation of liquid Zn in austenitization step. Zn-Al coating has a lower electro-chemical potential than GI coating, which leads to better cathodic corrosion protection. Therefore, dual Zn-Al coating overcomes most of the disadvantages of GI coating, including Zn evaporation, and LME.

Al-Si-Zn coating has been proposed by Hong et al. [ 173 ] The chemical composition of the dipping bath is Al-5 wt.% Si-24 wt.% Zn. After austenitization, a Zn-enriched zone formed in the surface structure, which effectively reduces the H intrusion by the hydrogen trapping effect of Zn. Although LME phenomenon is still observed at high temperature tensile testing, this harmful phenomenon is effectively prohibited by extending austenitization time to 6 min.

Although the application of coating systems effectively protects the martensite substrate from oxidation and corrosion, the introduction of coating brings side effects on PHS. It is reported that AlSi coating compromises the bendability and introduces extra hydrogen embrittlement risk to high strength PHS. This extra risk originates from the hydrogen uptake during the austenitization step. When the precoated steel sheet has been heated to austenitization temperature, Al on the top of precoating melts due to its low melting point and reacts intensively with the moisture in the furnace. This reaction produces massive hydrogen atoms or even hydrogen molecules. This hydrogen either disperses into the atmosphere or diffuses into the steel sheet through its surface structure. At elevated temperature, the diffusivity of hydrogen in the surface structure is large when compared to at room temperature. After the quenching, the temperature of the steel sheet cools down to room temperature, leading to the reduction hydrogen diffusivity of hydrogen in the materials. This hydrogen is trapped inside the martensite substrate of PHS due to the low hydrogen diffusivity at the surface structure.

Huang et al. [ 17 ] identified that as low as 0.37 ppm hydrogen could lead to serve bendability degradation of 2 GPa grade PHS. Considering this hydrogen content is low and easily reached in the industrial applications, this hydrogen embrittlement risk cannot be overlooked due to the safety concern. Figure  32 b has shown that noticeable degradation of bendability of AlSi coated PHS. While the bending angle of hydrogen-free sample is 39.1°, the bendability of sample with 0.37 ppm hydrogen is only 10.1°, which severely impairs the safe application of this high strength material. To mitigate the hydrogen embrittlement risk and promote the industrial application of 2 GPa grade high strength PHS, a new mechanism named surface plasticity-induced hydrogen delocalization has been proposed. Through a new heat treatment method, the surface structure of PHS has been dramatically changed. Large portion of brittle intermetallics like Fe 2 Al 5 , FeAl, FeAl/Fe 3 Al have been transformed to low-Al ferrite, which has much better plasticity. The demonstration of the surface structure plasticity enhancement has been shown in Fig.  33 . Due to the enhancement of surface plasticity, the formation of cracks on the surface structure is significantly restricted, thereby mitigating the hydrogen localization in the initiation stage of the critical crack that leads to the final fracture of PHS. During the crack propagation stage, the enhanced surface plasticity ensures relatively a large amount of plastic deformation happens ahead of the crack tip, which consumes crack propagation energy thereby restricting the propagation of the critical crack. Through this new proposed mechanism, the hydrogen embrittlement resistance of PHS is noticeably enhanced.
