sections.heading: Development of TWB
paragraphs: Currently, PHS has been widely applied in automotive industry due to its extremely high strength and great formability [ 9 ,  162 ], which effectively reduces the weight of BIW and improves the safety. Based on this advanced material, a new joining technique named tailor welded blank, which joins the PHS components with different strength, thickness, or even corrosion resistance, has been introduced into the automotive industry. TWB enables the engineers to have the maximum freedom to locally adjust the properties of the whole component by changing the welding segments. Through TWB technique, the best balance between mechanical performance, corrosion resistance, cost reduction and weight reduction is reached. The most widely used method to join the segments of TWB is by laser welding, and then the welded component is heated up for austenitization and subsequently quenched by one single stamping, which shortens the manufacturing process and cuts the cost. Although the application of TWB noticeably promotes the application of PHS in automotive industry and is one of the state-of-the-art techniques in automotive materials, it still has several drawbacks, which will be discussed in the following sections.

For PHS (22MnB5) without AlSi coating, the microstructure of raw base material is shown in Fig.  34 a. It consists of ferrite and pearlite. After the laser welding, the fusion zone (FZ) of the welding has been shown in Fig.  34 c, d. Due to the lack of extra elements, the FZ after welding consists of full martensite. After subsequent austenitization and quenching, the microstructure of FZ maintains the full martensitic structure. However, for PHS with AlSi coating, the microstructure of FZ becomes much more complex. Due to the melting of AlSi precoating and the diffusion of coating elements from the surface into FZ, the microstructure of FZ has been changed. The schematic for the diffusion process of precoating elements into FZ is shown in Fig.  35 . During the welding, the high temperature raised by laser melts both the base material and the precoating in the fusion zone. High temperature leads to the high diffusivity of precoating elements, therefore Al and Si diffuse from the surface into the molten pool as shown in Fig.  35 b. The diffusion of Al and Si changes the chemical composition of FZ. After cooling, the FZ becomes the mixture of martensite and ferrite due to the ferrite stabilization effect of Al. Figure  36  indicates the change of microstructure in both base material and the FZ of TWB. As the same of 22MnB5 without coating, the raw material consists of pearlite and ferrite (Fig.  36 a). After the heat treatment, the microstructure changes to full martensitic structure (Fig.  36 b). The microstructure of FZ right after the welding has been shown in Fig.  36 c. Due to the stabilization effect from Al and the extremely high temperature induced by laser welding, high temperature ferrite (δ-ferrite) forms in FZ. Martensite phase also coexists in the FZ. Through the heat treatment (austenitization and quenching), the microstructure of FZ has changed (Fig.  36 d). Due to the diffusion of elements during austenitization, low temperature ferrite (α-ferrite) and martensite coexist in the FZ. The existence of extra ferrite influences the mechanical properties of TWB. Ferrite is much softer and ductile than martensite, therefore it deforms much easier than the surrounding martensite. In the uniaxial tensile test, the deformation of ferrite leads to local stress concentration and results in the catastrophic failure of the material even at plastic regime. sections.heading: Hydrogen embrittlement of TWB
paragraphs: Study has shown that the wire filling welding improves the mechanical performance of TWB to some extent [ 174 ]. Wang et al. [ 174 ] compare the hydrogen embrittlement resistance of three different kinds of TWB: laser welding without filler wire (LW-HT), laser wire filling welding with post-weld heat treatment (LWF-HT), and laser wire filling welding with post-weld hot stamping (LWF-HS). When Al-Si coated steel is welded without a filler wire, the Al and Si from the coating melt into the weld pool. This leads to the formation of soft and brittle δ-ferrite alongside martensite in the FZ (Figs.  37 a and Fig.  38 a1, a2). The δ-ferrite significantly reduces the mechanical properties of the joint. Even without hydrogen charging, tensile specimens fracture in the FZ. The interface between δ-ferrite and martensite provides favorable sites for hydrogen accumulation, drastically increasing hydrogen embrittlement risk. For LWF-HS, the introduction of micro-alloyed filler wire (high in Ni and Cr) alters the chemical composition of the FZ. Ni stabilizes austenite, and Cr enhances hardenability, effectively suppressing the formation of δ-ferrite. The resulting FZ microstructure consists of martensite and retained austenite (RA) (Fig.  38 b). This transformation significantly strengthens the FZ, causing the base metal (BM) to become the weaker link and fracture point in the absence of, or under low hydrogen charging. However, the RA plays a dual role: it can trap hydrogen atoms, but under tensile stress, it may transform to martensite, inheriting a high local hydrogen concentration and triggering embrittlement. For LWF-HS, when the welded blank undergoes hot stamping (a process involving deformation and a slower cooling rate compared to direct quenching), the FZ microstructure is further optimized. Deformation refines the grains (Fig.  39 c shows a smaller grain size for LWF-HS), and the slower cooling rate promotes the precipitation of nano-scaled Fe₃C carbides within the martensitic matrix (Fig.  38 c). Both grain boundaries and these fine carbides act as strong, irreversible hydrogen traps. This microstructure demonstrates the highest resistance to hydrogen embrittlement, as fractures consistently occur in BM even under high hydrogen concentrations. The hydrogen induced brittle fracture of LWF-HT has been divided into three different conditions. At low hydrogen concentration (2–4 ppm), hydrogen primarily enhances localized plasticity. According to the HELP mechanism, hydrogen facilitates dislocation motion, leading to plastic deformation and the formation of shallow dimples on the fracture surface. In medium hydrogen concentration, the RA, which has trapped a substantial amount of hydrogen, transforms to martensite during tensile deformation. The newly formed martensite inherits this high hydrogen concentration, which severely reduces the interatomic bonding force. This leads to a brittle cleavage fracture within the FZ, as explained by the HEDE mechanism. At very high hydrogen levels, hydrogen saturates the prior austenite grain boundaries. The HEDE mechanism dominates, drastically reducing the grain boundary cohesion and resulting in a completely intergranular fracture. The FZ strength drops below that of the BM, causing the fracture location to shift from the BM to the FZ. In contrast, for the LWF-HS joint, even at a high hydrogen concentration, the hydrogen is effectively trapped at the numerous grain boundaries and nano-scaled carbides. This prevents a significant reduction in the cohesive strength of the grain boundaries and dislocation pinning force. Consequently, the FZ maintains higher strength than the BM, and the fracture remains in the BM with a dimpled morphology, showcasing excellent hydrogen embrittlement resistance.

sections.heading: Summary
paragraphs: This review discusses the critical challenge of hydrogen embrittlement in AHSS for automotive applications. This review covers the fundamental hydrogen embrittlement mechanisms, including hydrogen-enhanced decohesion and hydrogen-enhanced localized plasticity, and adsorption-induced dislocation emission. Then the advanced hydrogen distribution characterization techniques, such as TDS, SKPFM, APT and HMT have been discussed regarding their advantages and limitations. This review also discusses the current prevailing hydrogen embrittlement evaluation methods for industry and academic communities.

Across different steel grades, the hydrogen embrittlement sensitivity is fundamentally governed by characteristic microstructural features that control hydrogen trapping, diffusion, strain partitioning, and crack initiation. In Q&P steels, retained austenite is the key constituent with a dual role: it can act as an effective hydrogen trap and enhance ductility through the TRIP effect, but unstable austenite may transform into fresh martensite during deformation and thereby intensify local hydrogen concentration and crack initiation. In addition, martensite/austenite interfaces, martensite/ferrite interfaces, segregation bands, and fresh martensite formed during straining are all critical sites affecting hydrogen embrittlement sensitivity. In MMS, austenite engineering is the central strategy. The volume fraction, topology, morphology, and stability of austenite strongly influence whether hydrogen is trapped, redistributed, or concentrated in strain-localized regions. Beneficial features include chemically heterogeneous austenite, core–shell austenite, and elongated banded morphologies produced by warm rolling, because these structures can arrest crack propagation, reduce strain localization, or promote crack deflection and delamination. In PHS, the fully martensitic microstructure provides high strength but also high hydrogen embrittlement risk, mainly due to hydrogen segregation at PAGBs, high residual stress, and rapid hydrogen localization near critical defects. In this case, nano-carbides, reduced internal stress, and optimized surface structures are particularly important. For TWB, the fusion zone and heat-affected zone are the most vulnerable regions. Their hydrogen embrittlement sensitivity depends strongly on welding-induced microstructural heterogeneity, such as the formation of soft ferrite, retained austenite, refined grains, and nano-carbides, as well as on coating-derived chemical redistribution during welding.

Several general microstructural principles can be extracted from the above steel systems. Importantly, strong and irreversible hydrogen traps, such as fine Nb-, V-, and Mo-containing carbides, are highly effective in reducing diffusible hydrogen and improving hydrogen embrittlement resistance. Besides, microstructures that homogenize strain and suppress local stress concentration, such as dense multiple interfaces, refined phase distributions, and ferrite-enabled strain partitioning, are beneficial. Moreover, retained austenite should not be considered simply beneficial or detrimental: its effect depends on its stability, morphology, topology, and chemical heterogeneity. Film-like or chemically stabilized austenite is generally advantageous, whereas coarse blocky or mechanically unstable austenite can accelerate hydrogen-induced cracking. Finally, structural discontinuities such as segregation bands, brittle intermetallic surface layers, PAGBs, and weld-induced heterogeneous zones often dominate crack initiation and therefore must be specifically controlled.

Despite recent progress, several key challenges remain in hydrogen embrittlement research for automotive steels. Notably, hydrogen detection at the microstructural scale is still difficult because of the extremely low hydrogen concentration and high diffusivity in steel. Reliable hydrogen mapping often requires cryogenic conditions, indirect measurement, or deuterium substitution. Meanwhile, commonly used pre-charging methods may lead to nonuniform hydrogen distributions and hydrogen effusion during testing, which may lead to bias in hydrogen embrittlement assessment. In addition, most evaluation methods are still dominated by uniaxial tests, whereas real automotive components experience multiaxial stress states, residual stresses, bending, crash loading, and environment-assisted charging. Importantly, conclusions based only on steel grade names can be misleading, because steels with the same nominal grade may have very different alloy compositions and microstructures. Therefore, hydrogen embrittlement behavior should be discussed primarily from the standpoint of microstructural characteristics rather than nominal strength grade alone. Furthermore, the risk of hydrogen embrittlement remains extremely high in ultra-high-strength steels exceeding 2 GPa, especially in steels with a high martensite fraction.

For future research and alloy/process design, several directions appear particularly promising. From the viewpoint of alloying design, the introduction of finely dispersed carbide-forming elements such as Nb, V, and Mo should continue to be explored to create deep hydrogen traps, while boundary-strengthening elements such as B may help suppress hydrogen accumulation at PAGBs. In some systems, co-precipitation strategies and controlled elemental partitioning may also improve deformation compatibility between phases. From the viewpoint of microstructure tailoring, future work should focus on optimizing the stability, fraction, morphology, and topology of retained austenite; minimizing harmful segregation bands and coarse blocky constituents; constructing chemically heterogeneous or graded austenite; and refining phase distributions to improve strain partitioning and crack arrest capability. From the viewpoint of process measures, low-temperature tempering, flash annealing, intercritical annealing design, post-weld heat treatment, post-weld annealing, hot stamping under controlled atmosphere, and surface structure optimization all show clear potential.

In summary, the hydrogen embrittlement sensitivity of automotive AHSSs is not determined by strength level alone, but by the interplay among hydrogen transport, trapping hierarchy, strain localization, and crack-path microstructures. Therefore, future progress will rely on integrated design strategies that combine alloying design, microstructure tailoring, processing optimization, and realistic hydrogen embrittlement evaluation. Such a coordinated approach is essential for developing next-generation automotive steels that simultaneously satisfy the increasingly stringent requirements for strength, ductility, lightweighting, durability, and hydrogen embrittlement resistance.
